meta.tagline: The bayou city that commands space and sets the world's table

pills: The Houston of 'Houston, we have a problem'
Flavor capital from Viet-Cajun to fajitas

overview.title: Welcome to Houston
overview.intro: Houston carries two legends at once: the Mission Control room through which every command to the Moon passed, and America's most diverse table. This bayou city filled museums with oil money, enriched its kitchens through migration, grew without a plan and became free precisely because of it — nobody asks where you're from; they ask what we should eat. Rothko's silent chapel, the Menil's free collection, Asiatown's vast food halls and the skillets where the fajita was born share one map. H-Town doesn't show off; that's exactly why it's easy to love.

local_word.definition: Houston's homegrown nickname: a seal of belonging that moved from rap culture into daily speech. Whoever says 'H-Town proud' wears the city's unshowy pride. Houston doesn't describe itself with grand slogans but with these two syllables — nod when you hear it; you're included.

rules.title: Never plan a 'quick stop' at NASA
rules.description: Space Center Houston is 45 minutes from the center and wants a full day: the Mission Control tour (the Apollo-era room!) runs on timed trams, so book ahead. Go in the morning and set the tram tour early — the 'we'll be back in two hours' plan is this city's classic regret.

rules.title: Accept the car, tour neighborhood by neighborhood
rules.description: Houston is among America's most sprawling cities: a car is essential, the highway web vast, and the feeders confusing at first. The antidote is the neighborhood strategy — Montrose, the Museum District and the Heights are walkable within; cross between them at midday.

rules.title: Turn every meal into a world tour
rules.description: In Houston 'local cuisine' means the world: the fajita was born here, Viet-Cajun crawfish was invented here, and Asiatown sets some of America's best Chinese-Vietnamese tables. Give each meal another continent — the city's true museum is its menus.

quick_facts.label: Airport
quick_facts.sub: IAH the international giant, Hobby closer in

tip.label: The Houston philosophy
tip.text: This city is depth, not showcase: it reveals its beauty not from the freeway but from a museum garden, a taquería counter and a bayou path. Shift your expectations from views to tables — Houston conquers you at the table.

transport.title: Getting Around
transport.intro: Houston is an ocean of highways: the car is the base, METRORail works downtown, and the neighborhoods walk within themselves.

items.title: Arriving from the airports
items.description: Bush (IAH) is 35–50 minutes from the center: a ride app is the practical answer. Hobby is closer and calmer — prefer it for domestic arrivals. At both, budget for traffic hours.

items.title: The METRORail red line
items.description: The line from Downtown through the Museum District to the Medical Center is the corridor most useful to a visitor: on museum day, leave the car and take the train. Tickets from the platform machines.

items.title: The car and the feeder system
items.description: The 'feeder' roads running parallel to the freeways are a Houston specialty: miss your exit and you loop back on the feeder — no panic. Parking is plentiful and mostly easy; this city was built for the car.

items.title: The Buffalo Bayou paths
items.description: Kilometers of walking and cycling trails along the bayou that crosses the city: joggers, canoes and a bat colony against the Downtown skyline. Rent from the BCycle stations — Houston's greenest face.

items.title: The neighborhood strategy
items.description: Montrose, the Heights and Rice Village are walkable islands: park the car and tour on foot. In the Museum District nineteen museums line up within walking distance — Houston's most European corner.

callout.label: Bayou tip
callout.text: Before sunset, go to the Waugh Bridge in Buffalo Bayou Park: hundreds of thousands of bats pour out from under the bridge like a cloud at dusk. Then watch the Downtown skyline light up from the Eleanor Tinsley slope — Houston's best free show.

stay.title: Where to Stay
stay.intro: In Houston the choice is a choice of island: Montrose's bohemian streets, the Museum District's calm green, the Heights' bungalows or Downtown practicality.

local_word.definition: The local name for the 610 ring road circling the city: being 'Inside the Loop' means being in Houston's walkable, characterful core. It appears everywhere from real estate listings to small talk — for a visitor the translation is simple: stay inside the Loop, eat inside the Loop, and leave it only for NASA.

items.name: Montrose
items.description: Art galleries, vintage shops, tattoo parlors and the city's best restaurant density: Houston's free-spirited quarter. The Menil and Rothko within walking distance — the address for character seekers.

items.name: Museum District
items.description: The neighborhood of nineteen museums and Hermann Park: museum mornings, park picnics at noon, quiet evenings. On the METRORail — the natural base for a culture-first visit.

items.name: The Heights
items.description: Victorian bungalows, antique shops and the neighborhood stores of 19th Street: Houston's small-town-textured corner. Strong craft beer and brunch scenes — a stay at local rhythm.

items.name: Downtown
items.description: The tunnel-linked business district comes alive on game and concert nights: Minute Maid and the Toyota Center next door. At the rail junction — a sensible base for an event-focused visit.

items.name: Rice Village and West U
items.description: A shop-and-cafe district beside Rice University's oak-lined campus: calm, safe, walkable. The balanced choice for family- and comfort-first stays.

best_time.title: When to Go
best_time.intro: Houston's calendar is a bargain with humidity: November to April is the golden window, summer is a sauna, and March means the Rodeo.

items.label: Spring
items.name: Rodeo and Bluebonnets
items.subtitle: Spring · The world's biggest rodeo, mild evenings
items.description: March means the Houston Livestock Show and Rodeo: three weeks of concerts, barbecue contests and real rodeo. April and May run mild and green — the bayou trails' finest season.

callout.label: Rodeo tip
callout.text: Go to the Rodeo on a weekday: livestock barns and barbecue first, rodeo and a concert at night. Tickets and hotels price up in rodeo weeks — check the dates early.

items.label: Summer
items.name: Sauna Season
items.subtitle: Summer · Humidity + heat, icy interiors
items.description: A Houston summer is a humid sauna: brutal outdoors at noon, freezing indoors. Museums, the aquarium and the Asiatown food halls are the season's natural route — an evening bayou walk remains as the reward.

callout.label: Humidity note
callout.text: Don't force outdoor plans at summer noon: even a two-block walk soaks you. Build the day before 09:00 and after 19:00 — museum chill is your best friend between. And review the August–September hurricane calendar.

items.label: Autumn
items.name: Humidity's Farewell
items.subtitle: Autumn · Mild dry days, open-air season
items.description: In October the humidity breaks and Houston steps outside: bayou picnics, open-air concerts and porch tables. November is this city's secret peak month — sweet air, no crowds, kitchens at full strength.

callout.label: November tip
callout.text: Spend a November afternoon on the Menil campus: the collection is free, the lawns welcome picnics, and the Rothko Chapel is two steps away. Houston's most graceful half day hides on this campus.

items.label: Winter
items.name: Soft and Open
items.subtitle: Winter · 18°C days, rare cold snaps
items.description: Houston winter is mostly jacket-weather and sunny: the open-air program runs year-round. Now and then a sudden freeze startles the city — but most winter days offer the sweet climate the North flees toward.

callout.label: January tip
callout.text: Do your Space Center day on a mild winter morning: crowds low, tram tour calm, longer minutes in the Mission Control room. Hot pho in Asiatown on the way back — that's the winter Houston formula.

eat.title: What to Eat
eat.intro: Houston is America's table capital: birthplace of the fajita, invention house of Viet-Cajun, port of Gulf oysters — here the menu is a passport.

local_word.definition: The soft-dough morning pastry Czech immigrants brought to Texas: the fruit-filled original is sweet, and the sausage-jalapeño Texan take — the 'klobasnek' — is legend. A Houston morning starts with a kolache box — when you see a bakery queue, join it and buy a variety.

items.name: Fajitas
items.description: Skirt steak on a sizzling skillet with tortillas and guacamole: the fajita was born in this city and the recipe is still best here. As the smoke rises from the pan, the wrapping art is yours — stay true to the onion-and-pepper classic.

items.name: Viet-Cajun crawfish
items.description: The Houston invention born when Vietnamese immigrants added garlic butter and lemongrass to the Cajun crawfish boil: gloves on, bib tied, dive into the crawfish poured across the table. The season peaks in spring.

items.name: The kolache morning
items.description: A box of sausage-and-cheese klobasneks and fruit kolaches: the Texas-Czech classic of the road breakfast. Bought by the dozen from a morning bakery — office, road or hotel; diplomacy ends when the box opens.

items.name: Houston barbecue
items.description: Beside brisket and ribs, this city's difference is variety: boudin-stuffed, Tex-Mex-inflected, kolache-wrapped barbecue interpretations. The lunchtime queue rule applies here too.

items.name: Gulf oysters
items.description: Galveston Bay oysters on ice or over coals: lemon and Tabasco, not mignonette, is the local way. Oyster-bar happy hour is Houston's best affordable luxury.

items.name: The Asiatown food halls
items.description: Along Bellaire Boulevard, some of America's best Vietnamese, Chinese and Malaysian tables: pho in the morning, dim sum at noon, banh mi at night. In the vast food halls the menus are generous and the prices friendly — dedicate a day.

callout.label: Table rule
callout.text: In Houston you don't need a famous window: the plain restaurant in a strip mall is often the city's best. A queue, full family tables and a menu devoted to one kitchen — these three signs never mislead in Houston.

hidden_gems.title: Hidden Corners
hidden_gems.intro: Everyone knows the Space Center; these six are Houston's silent, artful, surprising hidden face.

items.name: The Rothko Chapel
items.description: An octagonal meditation chapel ringed by fourteen vast Rothko canvases: no sound inside, only light and deep violet. It silences everyone regardless of faith — Houston's deepest half hour, free.

items.name: The Menil Collection campus
items.description: A museum campus built on oil wealth and entirely free: from the Surrealists to Byzantine icons, set among lawns. The Cy Twombly gallery and the bungalow streets included — America's most graceful art island.

items.name: The Buffalo Bayou Cistern
items.description: A 1926 underground reservoir: 221 concrete columns, mirror-still water and cathedral acoustics. Entered by guided tour, with rotating art installations — Houston's most unexpected space.

items.name: Smither Park
items.description: A folk-art park woven from salvage and mosaic by hundreds of artists: every panel by a different hand. Together with the Orange Show next door — a monument to Houston's 'weird and wonderful' tradition.

items.name: The Asiatown (Bellaire) crawl
items.description: Food halls, bakeries, boba shops and giant markets along an eight-kilometer boulevard: among America's liveliest Asian corridors. On Saturday noon the dim sum halls become a feast.

items.name: Eleanor Tinsley Park
items.description: The slope of Buffalo Bayou directly facing the Downtown skyline: picnickers, canoeists and sunset photographers. Also the main stage of the July 4th fireworks — the city's postcard is shot from this grass.

callout.label: Quiet-loud strategy
callout.text: Build the Houston day on contrast: Rothko's silence in the morning, Asiatown's hum at noon, the bats over the bayou at dusk. This city can't be toured in one tone — it opens as the tones change.

traps.title: Tourist Traps
traps.intro: Houston is modest and honest; its traps grow from misjudged scale — know these four.

items.name: The 'we'll swing by NASA' plan
items.description: The Space Center is 45 minutes from the center and the tram tours are timed: the afternoon arrival goes home without seeing Mission Control.
items.instead: Give it a full day, book the ticket and tram tour ahead, go in the morning. The restored Apollo Mission Control room is the trip's summit — returning without it is seeing half of Houston.

items.name: The walkability assumption
items.description: The map says 'close'; the shadeless feeders and mega-blocks say no: walking between points in Houston is often simply impossible.
items.instead: Walk within the island neighborhoods (Montrose, the Heights, the Museum District) and drive between them. For museum day, METRORail beats the car — nineteen museums with no parking worries.

items.name: The tourist 'Gulf seafood' window
items.description: Some aquarium-restaurant windows sell frozen shrimp at Gulf prices: there's a view, but no freshness.
items.instead: Eat oysters at the storied oyster bars and crawfish in season at the Viet-Cajun halls. Don't sit anywhere that can't answer 'which bay are today's oysters from?'

items.name: Ignoring hurricane season
items.description: In August and September the tropical-storm risk is real: the unprepared visitor meets cancellations and closures.
items.instead: In those months buy travel insurance, choose flexible flights and keep the weather feed on. If a storm is distant, no panic — Houston's infrastructure is strong; watch the locals and follow instructions.

callout.label: Golden rule
callout.text: The only source of disappointment in Houston is the wrong expectation: seekers of showcase tire; seekers of tables and art rejoice. Shrink the plan, grow the appetite — H-Town repays with interest.

itinerary.title: Ready-Made Itineraries
itinerary.intro: If you hate planning, follow these flows. Times are flexible; keep the spirit, break the order.

plans.title: If You Have 1 Day
plans.subtitle: From the silent chapel to the bat cloud

steps.title: Kolache breakfast
steps.description: A mixed box from the bakery: sausage klobasneks and fruit kolaches. Large coffee — a Houston morning opens this way.

steps.title: The Menil and Rothko
steps.description: A morning tour of the free collection, then half an hour of silence in the Rothko Chapel: Houston's spiritual core.

steps.title: Fajita lunch
steps.description: Skirt steak on a sizzling skillet, tortilla in hand: eat the fajita in its birthplace.

steps.title: Museum District hours
steps.description: The dinosaur hall of the natural science museum or the fine arts: nineteen options, one neighborhood. Catch your breath in Hermann Park.

steps.title: Buffalo Bayou and the bats
steps.description: A walk on the bayou path, the dusk bat cloud at Waugh Bridge, and the skyline from Eleanor Tinsley.

steps.title: Asiatown finale
steps.description: Pho or Viet-Cajun crawfish on Bellaire Boulevard: gloves, bib and full tables — a Houston night.

plans.title: If You Have 3 Days
plans.subtitle: Space, art and a world table — the full H-Town

steps.title: Classic Houston
steps.description: The 1-day flow above: kolaches, the Menil-Rothko, fajitas, museums, the bayou, Asiatown.

steps.title: Space Center day
steps.description: Hit the road early: the Mission Control tram tour, the Saturn V rocket and the shuttle exhibit — a full day. Gulf oysters for dinner on the way back; a Downtown game or concert if energy remains.

steps.title: Neighborhoods and weird wonders
steps.description: Bungalow streets and antique shops in the Heights in the morning; the barbecue queue at noon; Smither Park mosaics + the Cistern guided tour in the afternoon; farewell dinner on Montrose's best restaurant streets.

phrases.title: 5-Word Survival Kit
phrases.intro: Houston English is Texas sweetness mixed with the world's accents; these five warm the city to you.

items.meaning: Houston's nickname — use it and the local smiles
You all — Texas's official pronoun, valid currency here too
The highway frontage road — 'take the feeder' is Houston-only navigation
Hello — the Texas greeting; comes with a nod
Houston's candy-paint, swangin'-wheels classic car culture — salute one when you see it

checklist.completion_message: H-Town proud! You've lived the city of space and the table the way it deserves!
